chunks: Muhammad ibn Ja'far al-Razzaz, from Muhammad ibn Isa, from Ali ibn Mahziyar, similar to it.

And he wrote to him, 'O my master! A man vowed to fast on Friday permanently for the remainder of his life. That day coincided with Eid al-Fitr, or Eid al-Adha, or the days of Tashreeq, or travel, or illness. Is the fast of that day upon him, or its fulfillment, or what should he do, O my master?' So he wrote to him, 'Allah has relieved him of fasting on all these days, and he should fast one day in exchange for one day, if Allah wills.'

And he wrote to him, asking him, 'O my master! A man vowed to fast a day, and that day coincided with his having relations with his wife. What is upon him regarding the expiation?' So he wrote to him, 'He should fast one day in exchange for one day, and free a believing slave.'
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling for a vow to fast on Fridays that falls on days of Eid or travel?
ai.summary: In this narration from al-Kafi, Imam al-Rida (or the Imam depending on the specific chain context, often attributed to Imam al-Rida in this specific Qaḍāʾ context) clarifies that a perpetual vow to fast on Friday is not annulled by the occurrence of exemptive days (Eid, Tashreeq, travel, illness) but rather suspended, requiring only a single compensatory fast (qaḍāʾ) for each missed Friday. Furthermore, if the vow coincides with marital relations, the ruling specifies a dual expiation: fasting one day and freeing a believing slave, reflecting the Shia juristic view that the vow's obligation persists despite the temporary prohibition of fasting. This highlights the distinction between the prohibition of fasting on specific days and the suspension of a vowed obligation, a key nuance in Usuli fiqh.
